title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates the effect of deterministic post‑processing (a NetOps verifier + lightweight topology simulator) on deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcomes when the same single LLM candidate is reused verbatim across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks (600 episodes); completed: 598 episodes → 299 complete pairs. For the 299 analyzable pairs the archived contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; both baseline and guarded arms accepted the identical candidates (299/299). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and execution logs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes (see Disclosure). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics this run shows no downstream‑postprocessing effect on the deterministic validator verdict for identical candidates; it does not address whether independent tool‑augmented generation would change generation quality or safety.

sections.introduction: Motivation and scope. Generative LLMs are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and configuration repair. Architectures that pair generation with deterministic validators, simulators, or repair loops are intended to improve operational correctness. Empirical evaluations, however, often mix improvements due to (A) higher‑quality generation versus (B) deterministic post‑processing and repair. We designed a preregistered experiment to isolate (B): when the exact same LLM candidate is supplied to both pipelines, can deterministic post‑processing (verifier + simulator) change the deterministic validator pass/fail verdict? This paper reports the preregistered design, the complete execution and analysis artifacts, the exact observed contingency and statistical assessment, representative validator traces, and implications for follow‑up designs.
sections.related_work: Positioning. Prior work motivates and contextualizes the present narrow question: intent→configuration translation and constrained generation (Nguyen et al., 2024, doi:10.1002/nem.2313), pretrained configuration models and corpora (PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369), tool‑augmented agent architectures and RAG agents in operations (preprints and domain work, e.g., 10.20944/preprints202604.1820.v1), and operational verifier/runtime reliability studies (e.g., WeClaw‑style runtime work and verifier tradeoffs, 10.2139/ssrn.7317098; domain firewall tooling 10.5220/0013221900003890). These sources motivated: (i) rigorous preregistration, (ii) artifact hashing and archival, and (iii) isolating generation vs post‑processing effects. We cite only verified records (manuscript_evidence_bundle.cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) before execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator pass indicator. Design semantics (frozen): shared_initial_candidate — for each task a single LLM generation was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines. Sampling and power. Planned n=300 pairs (150 simple, 150 complex). Power calculation (pre‑lock) targeted detecting a 0.20 absolute paired difference assuming baseline ≈0.60, α=0.05, power=0.90; the observed baseline rate differed (see Results). Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Generation budget: one shared generation per task; maximum model_calls pre‑registered = 600. Verifier/simulator. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) canonically parses candidate commands, enforces per‑task workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore), runs a lightweight topology simulation to compute final_state snapshots, and emits violation codes. Validation outputs include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, final_state, and difficulty metadata. Preregistered missingness and contamination rules. Exact‑string matches to a public config corpus would be excluded from confirmatory analysis; provider failures are logged and complete‑pair rules applied (artifacted). Archival, hashing, and provenance. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, execution and analysis logs were archived and SHA‑256 hashed (execution/*). Representative artifact paths and hashes are given in the Disclosure.
sections.results: Execution summary (artifact‑grounded). Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (forming one missing pair); complete analyzable pairs = 299 (execution/execution_manifest.json; see execution manifest hashes). Model calls used = 300. Primary confirmatory outcome (archived analysis): the exact paired contingency for the 299 analyzable pairs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43abf83e081bb5a3c3a21fa0de67afd72628ee5ed880f2bff810e627174) is: n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Baseline success rate = 299/299 (100.0%); guarded success rate = 299/299 (100.0%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI = [0.00,0.00] (artifact: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Representative scored episodes. Each scored episode is archived as a per‑task scoring JSON containing: normalized_response, raw_response_sha256, validator_trace with final_state and difficulty metadata. Example representative artifacts: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (sha256: 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256: 6569b491...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha256: cefa6344...). Missingness and failures. The one excluded pair (pair‑000269) corresponds to failed provider calls for the shared_initial generation; the provider failure event and its provider trace are archived (execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json) and the execution log records the event (execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8). Per preregistered rules the pair was excluded from the primary complete‑pair analysis; all failure artifacts and the exact failure JSON are archived for audit.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and scope. The experiment answers a narrow, preregistered question: when the exact same single LLM candidate is reused by both pipelines, deterministic verifier+simulator post‑processing did not change the deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcome for the analyzable confirmatory sample (299/299 concordant acceptances). This is a factual, artifact‑anchored result; it does not imply that validators or simulators are operationally unnecessary. Validators produce explicit violation codes, final_state snapshots, and reproducible audit trails — value that remains independent of whether they change a pass/fail decision in this specific shared‑candidate scenario. Ceiling effect and design consequences. The preregistered power assumption (baseline ≈0.60) was not met: observed baseline success was 1.00, producing a ceiling effect that makes the originally targeted minimally important effect (+0.20) unobservable in this execution. Consequences: (1) the null paired difference is exact in the completed sample but non‑informative about effects that could exist when baseline success is lower; (2) follow‑up designs should (A) adopt independent per‑condition generation (not shared candidate reuse), (B) include adversarial or higher‑difficulty strata to avoid ceiling, and (C) replicate across model families and seeds. Operational implications. For operational deployment, three points follow from these artifact‑grounded observations: (i) If generation quality is high (as in our confirmatory set), downstream deterministic validation may be a confirmatory audit step more than a corrective operator; (ii) validators remain essential for auditability, explicit violation coding, and simulator‑based final_state snapshots; (iii) experiments that aim to measure whether tool‑augmented agents improve generation must let generation vary by condition. Reproducibility and artifact availability. Every numeric claim above is reproducible from the archived artifacts: execution/execution_manifest.json (full artifact manifest and per‑file SHA‑256s), execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/*.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/*.csv and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg. The exact preregistration and master prompt immutable references are included in the Disclosure. Limitations and threats to validity. We discuss construct, internal, external and conclusion validity explicitly in the Limitations section below and archive all supporting artifacts.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired run that fixed generation (shared_initial_candidate) found no difference between baseline and guarded pipelines on the preregistered estimand: both accepted the identical candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs (n11=299). The result is narrowly scoped and artifact‑traceable; it does not speak to independent tool‑augmented generation. We provide complete provenance (raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, analysis artifacts and SHA‑256 manifests) to enable audit and replication, and we propose concrete preregistration recommendations for follow‑ups that evaluate independent tool‑augmented generation.

limitations: The confirmatory design used shared_initial_candidate semantics and therefore isolates only downstream post‑processing effects; it cannot assess whether tool‑augmented generation (i.e., allowing the agent to call verifiers/simulators during generation or to produce repaired candidates) would improve generation quality or safety.

Tasks were drawn from a deterministic synthetic topology pool and executed in a lightweight topology simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, device firmware idiosyncrasies, or production telemetry is limited.
Only a single declared model family (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or seeds without replication.

The deterministic validator encodes a curated rule set and workflow invariants (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that are a proxy for operational correctness but cannot exhaustively represent all production hardware behaviors or operator policies.

A ceiling effect occurred (observed baseline success 100%): the preregistered power assumptions were not met and the experiment could not detect the preregistered minimally important paired difference (0.20).
